opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of the core tensions we've been trying to resolve. Right now there's essentially a binary choice. You either open-source your model, which is great for research, reproducibility, and people building on top of it, but then you have almost no way to capture value from it. Or you keep it closed behind an API, which lets you monetize but means nobody can inspect it, verify what it's doing, or really build on it in a deep way. That pushes the whole industry toward a few large companies that can afford to train and then lock everything up.

What decentralized confidential machine learning lets you do is break that binary. The model weights can be encrypted and run inside secure enclaves, trusted execution environments on GPUs and CPUs, so the computation happens on hardware where neither the operator of the machine nor the user can extract the weights. But you can still prove what model is running and that the inference was done correctly. So a researcher or a small team can publish a model, let anyone use it, and actually get paid every time it's used, without handing over the weights for free.

The same thing works in the other direction for data. Users can send their data encrypted, it gets processed inside the enclave, and the model owner never sees it. That's a big deal, because a lot of the most valuable data, like medical records, financial information, or personal context, is exactly what people won't share with a centralized provider.

Once you have that, you can build collaboration structures that weren't possible before. Multiple parties can contribute data, compute, or fine-tuning work to a shared model, and because everything is tracked and verifiable, you can attribute contributions and split revenue. You can have open research in the sense that the architecture, training process, and evaluations are transparent and auditable, while the economic value isn't immediately captured by whoever copies the weights first.

For me, this is really about making sure AI doesn't end up concentrated in a few hands. If the only way to get paid for building a great model is to be a giant closed lab, that's what we'll get. If anyone can contribute and get rewarded through an open, verifiable network, you get a much healthier ecosystem, and ultimately AI that's actually aligned with the users it serves rather than with whoever controls the servers.

r001.rationale: The response says encrypted weights run inside secure enclaves and that a model creator can let anyone use the model while getting paid for each use.

r002.rationale: It mentions payment and revenue sharing, but does not propose a usage surcharge above compute costs.

r003.rationale: It says anyone can use a published model, but does not state that users can keep using it without anyone being able to stop access.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought about a lot, because the tension is real. Right now you basically have two camps. You have the fully open-weights world, where you publish the model and anybody can download it, run it, fine-tune it, and that's great for research and collaboration, but it's very hard to capture value, so the people doing the work either need a big sponsor or they need to pivot to a closed API business. And then you have the closed world, where the model sits behind an API, you can monetize it, but nobody can inspect it, nobody can build on top of it in a meaningful way, and all the trust goes to a single company.

What we're trying to do with the DCML approach, decentralized confidential machine learning, is to break that trade-off. The core idea is that the model weights are encrypted, and they're only ever decrypted inside a trusted execution environment, so a confidential computing enclave. Inference happens inside that enclave. The node operator running the hardware can't see the weights, the user can't see the weights, but both of them can get a cryptographic attestation that says, this is exactly the model that was published, running exactly the code that was published, and nothing else is going on.

So now think about what that unlocks. A researcher or a small lab can publish a model and attach a payment rule to it. Every time someone runs inference against it, a fee goes back to whoever contributed to the model. That can be the original authors, it can be the people who provided data, it can be someone who fine-tuned it, because you can have composability where a fine-tune references a base model and the revenue gets split by the rules encoded on-chain. The weights never leak, so you don't have the problem where the moment you release something, it's cloned and the economic incentive disappears.

At the same time, it's still open in the ways that matter for science. You can publish the architecture, the training recipe, the evals. You can let other people run experiments against the model, probe it, build agents on top of it, even fine-tune it inside the same confidential environment without ever extracting the weights. So collaboration is not "here is a zip file," it's "here is a verifiable, composable object that you can build on, and the attribution and payments are handled by the protocol instead of by a licensing department."

And I think the important part is that this also solves a trust problem for users. When you use a closed API today, you have no idea what model you're actually talking to, whether it got swapped, whether your data is being logged. With attestation and decentralized infrastructure, you get privacy for your prompts and verifiability of the model at the same time. So you get the monetization story that lets independent teams actually sustain themselves, you get the openness that lets the research community move faster, and you get a user who doesn't have to just trust a logo. That combination is really what we mean by user-owned AI.

r001.rationale: It says encrypted weights are decrypted only inside a confidential execution enclave, where inference runs, and proposes charging a fee for each inference.

r002.rationale: It proposes per-inference fees for authors and contributors, but does not say the fee is a surcharge above compute costs.

r003.rationale: It describes experimentation and building on models, but does not claim users can keep using them without anyone being able to stop them.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is separating sharing knowledge from giving away all the value of running a model. You can publish the research and collaborate on improving the approach, while keeping the trained model encrypted. Then, through DCML, people could pay to use that model without receiving the underlying weights, and the people contributing the model or the computation could be compensated.

That creates a potential business model around use, rather than requiring everybody to keep their research secret. But encryption alone doesn’t solve everything. You still need a way to execute the model without exposing it, verify that the computation was performed correctly, and work out how contributors get paid. If we can make those pieces work together, open collaboration and monetization become much more compatible.

r001.rationale: It says the trained model can stay encrypted and people can pay to use it through DCML without receiving its underlying weights.

r002.rationale: It says contributors could be compensated, but does not specify funding them through a usage surcharge above compute costs.

r003.rationale: It discusses paid access and open collaboration, but does not claim users can keep using the models without anyone being able to stop them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is separating access to the research from access to the computation. You want people to share ideas, publish results, and build on each other’s work. But if somebody has invested in training a useful model, they also need a way to get paid when people use it.

With an encrypted model running through DCML, the idea is that you can make the model available for computation without handing over the weights. Someone submits an input, pays for the execution, and gets a result. That payment can support both the person who contributed the model and the people providing the compute.

That doesn’t automatically make the model open research—you still have to decide what to publish and how other researchers can reproduce your results. But it gives you another way to monetize beyond keeping everything inside a company and selling access through your own service. You can collaborate on the research and still have an economic incentive to contribute useful models.

r001.rationale: It says the encrypted model can be used for computation without giving users the weights, and that users pay to submit inputs and receive results.

r002.rationale: It says payments can support model contributors and compute providers, but does not propose a usage surcharge above compute costs.

r003.rationale: It describes an alternative to a company’s own service, but does not claim users can keep using the model without anyone being able to stop them.
